newsitem.title: GERMANY: Lavish liquidity forces German call money lower.
newsitem.headline: Lavish liquidity forces German call money lower.

text.p: Lavish liquidity conditions helped push German overnight funds still lower on Friday to trade under the Bundesbank's main money market rate, signalling the central bank is doing all it can to keep rates from rising.
"Rates dipped still lower even though our reserve holdings were also smaller, that is very remarkable," one dealer said.

After trading exactly at the main money market rate of three percent on Thursday, call money on Friday traded between 3.00 and 2.95 percent with the bulk of trades conducted at 2.97 percent, dealers said. Dealers said rates might even slip further this afternoon.

Banks' holdings at the Bundesbank slipped to 39.1 billion marks on Thursday from Wednesday's 40.4 billion mark level. The monthly average rate also slipped, standing now at 40.2 billion marks after 40.4 billion marks on day earlier.
Dealers were slightly concerned about holding excessive amounts of funds over the weekend and said efforts to get rid of money before the end of trading could still help send rates lower.
As the central bank has allowed money market rates to trade ever closer to the repo, dealers said this new practice is likely designed to prevent any rate hike fears from emerging.

"They want to make very sure that no one gets the idea they are on the verge of raising rates again," something which could be interpreted as a death blow the Europe's planned currency union, another dealer added.

But dealers also said they expected rates to rise slightly again next week, leaving no reason for the Bundesbank to enter the market and drain funds. "It will all sort itself out next week," a dealer predicted.
On Friday the Frankfurt Interbank Offered Rate FIONA= was set at 3.01333 percent while it was at 3.03475 percent Thursday. --Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525
